meta.title: ABF Standard Five-Card Majors
meta.system: Joan Butts / ABF teaching Standard 5CM, Stayman and Jacoby transfers
meta.source: ABF Standard System Card (Joan Butts teaching dialect)

chapters.title: Opening the bidding
chapters.summary: Count your points, decide whether to open, then pick the right suit. 5-card majors, minors by length.
concepts: Suits rank low to high: ♣ clubs, ♦ diamonds, ♥ hearts, ♠ spades — then notrump above all four.
♥ and ♠ are the major suits; ♣ and ♦ are the minors. Game is 4♥/4♠ (ten tricks) but 5♣/5♦ (eleven), so the system hunts for a major fit first and treats the minors as a starting bid.
Step 1 — count HCP: A=4, K=3, Q=2, J=1.
Step 2 — add length: +1 for a five-card suit, +2 for a six, +3 for a seven. HCP + length = your opening points.
Step 3 — 13+ opening points: open. Otherwise Step 4 — Rule of 20: HCP + your longest suit + your second-longest suit ≥ 20, with at least 10 HCP.
1♥/1♠ promise 5+ cards. 1♦ is 4+; 1♣ is 3+.
5–5 or 6–6: higher ranking. 6–5: the six. 4–4 minors: 1♦. 3–3 minors: 1♣.

chapters.title: Notrump and strong openings
chapters.summary: Balanced 15–17 opens 1NT (even with a 5-card major). Stronger balanced hands jump; huge hands start with 2♣.
concepts: 1NT = 15–17 HCP balanced (4333 / 4432 / 5332), including a 5-card major.
14 HCP balanced with a 5-card suit upgrades to 1NT. 5422 is not balanced.
2NT = 20–21 balanced. 2♣ = 22+ HCP, or 21+ opening points unbalanced.

chapters.title: Preempts
chapters.summary: With a long suit and a weak hand that cannot open at the one-level, get in the way: weak two or a three-level preempt — except in fourth seat, where there is no room left to steal.
concepts: Weak 2♦/♥/♠ = exactly 6 cards, 5–10 HCP, cannot open one-level. No weak 2♣.
7+ cards, 5–10 HCP, cannot open: preempt at the 3-level in any suit.
Fourth seat: no preempt — three passes in front means there is nobody left to shut out.

chapters.title: Responding to 1NT
chapters.summary: After partner's strong 1NT, count HCP only. Transfer with a five-card major; Stayman with a four-card major and 8+; otherwise Pass / 2NT / 3NT.
concepts: HCP only — no length points as responder to 1NT.
10+ and no 4-card major: 3NT. 8–9: 2NT (invitational). Else Pass.
5+ major: transfer (2♦ → hearts, 2♥ → spades). 5–5 majors: transfer to spades.
4-card major (or 5–4 majors) and 8+, no 5-card major: Stayman. Garbage Stayman is off.

chapters.title: Responding to 1♥ or 1♠
chapters.summary: Fit first. With 3+ support, limit-raise using HCP + shortage. Without a fit, bid a suit if you can afford it, else 1NT or pass.
concepts: 3+ support: 0–5 pass, 6–9 raise to 2, 10–12 jump to 3, 13+ raise to game.
Shortage points with a fit: doubleton +1, singleton +3, void +5.
No fit: a new suit at the one-level is 6+ HCP; at the two-level, 10+ (5+ cards for a new major).
6–9, no fit, nothing biddable: 1NT. 0–5: Pass.

chapters.title: Responding to 1♣ or 1♦
chapters.summary: Partner's minor may be short, so a major of your own comes first. No major: 1♦ over 1♣, 2♣ on six clubs over 1♦, else notrump or pass.
concepts: Majors first (4+ cards, 6+ HCP), cheaper of 4–4 majors.
1♣–1♦ = 4+ diamonds, 6+ HCP, no 4-card major.
1♦–2♣ = 6+ clubs and 10+ HCP — a two-level new suit.
Raise 1♣ with 5+ clubs, 1♦ with 4+ diamonds. 13+ HCP? 3NT, not five of a minor — unless you are unbalanced with 16+.
6–9 balanced, no major: 1NT. 0–5: Pass.

chapters.title: Opener’s rebid
chapters.summary: After partner responds, describe strength and shape: pass a minimum, invite or bid game with extra, and always complete Stayman and transfers.
concepts: After a raise of our major: 13–15 pass, 16–18 raise one, 19–20 bid game (opening points).
After 1NT: pass 5332 minimum; rebid a 6-card suit; show a 4-card side suit.
After Stayman: 2♥ with 4 hearts (even with 4 spades), 2♠ with 4 spades and no 4 hearts, else 2♦.
After a transfer: always complete. No super-accept in this tree.

chapters.title: Opener's rebid after a new suit
chapters.summary: A new suit from partner is forcing for one round — you must bid again. Show a fit, repeat a long suit, or fall back on notrump by strength. An invitation you may pass, but only on a minimum.
concepts: A new suit by responder is forcing for one round. Opener may not pass it.
Priority: support partner’s suit → repeat your own 6-card suit → notrump by strength.
Over a one-level response you can still show a four-card major at the one level — do that first.
A two-level response promises 10+, so the pair is near game: minimum bids 2NT, extras bid 3NT.
An invitation (2NT, or a limited raise) may be passed — but only on a minimum, never on autopilot.

chapters.title: Answering the big and the weak openings
chapters.summary: 2♣, 2NT and the preempts each tell you almost everything in one bid. What you say back depends on which: 2♣ you may never pass, 2NT you treat like a bigger 1NT, and a weak two you raise, pass, or drive to game — while over a three-level preempt it is game or nothing.
concepts: 2♣ is game-forcing. Pass is never legal: 2♦ is the waiting bid with 0–7.
8+ with a five-card suit is a positive response to 2♣ — name the suit.
2NT (20–21) takes Stayman and transfers a level higher: 3♣ asks, 3♦ → hearts, 3♥ → spades.
Over 2NT the bar drops: 5+ HCP is 3NT, because partner has 20.
A weak two or a preempt is limited, so responder is the captain: bid game with 16+, raise a weak two to obstruct, or pass.
Opener does not bid again over a limited opening unless partner bids a new suit.

lessons.title: When you pass
lessons.tip: If you cannot open at the one-level and you do not have a weak two or a seven-card preempt, pass.
lessons.newHere: The four suits and how they rank, majors versus minors, and the whole point count: HCP, length points, the 13-point test and the Rule of 20.
teaching: First, the suits. They rank low to high: ♣ clubs, ♦ diamonds, ♥ hearts, ♠ spades, and notrump sits above all four. Hearts and spades are the major suits; clubs and diamonds are the minor suits. The names matter because game in a major is 4♥ or 4♠ — ten tricks — while game in a minor is 5♣ or 5♦, eleven tricks. A major game is a whole trick cheaper, so this system spends its energy looking for an eight-card major fit, and opens a minor mostly to get the auction started.

An opening bid is the first real bid of the auction: the first call that is not Pass. It is not “the first time you speak.” If you are dealer and you pass, you have not opened — you have said you do not have an opening hand. If everyone passes, the deal is passed out and nobody opened.

Now count, in this order, every single hand. Step 1: high-card points — Ace 4, King 3, Queen 2, Jack 1. Step 2: length points — add one for every card past the fourth in a suit, so a five-card suit is +1, a six is +2, a seven is +3. HCP plus length is your opening points.

Step 3: if that total is 13 or more, you have an opening hand. Step 4: if it is not, and you hold at least 10 HCP, try the Rule of 20 — add your HCP to the length of your longest suit and the length of your second-longest suit. Reach 20 and you may open; fall short and you pass.

Step 5: with neither, pass. One exception exists and it is worth knowing the shape of now: a very long suit with a weak hand bids anyway, to get in the way — exactly six diamonds, hearts or spades with 5–10 HCP, or seven or more cards in any suit with 5–10 HCP. Lesson 6 drills those. Every hand in this lesson fails that test too, so here the answer is always Pass.
rules: Majors = ♥ ♠ (game is 10 tricks). Minors = ♣ ♦ (game is 11). Suit rank: ♣ < ♦ < ♥ < ♠ < NT.
Opening bid = the first non-pass call of the auction, whoever makes it.
Step 1: HCP — A=4, K=3, Q=2, J=1.
Step 2: length — +1 for a 5-card suit, +2 for a 6, +3 for a 7. HCP + length = opening points.
Step 3: 13+ opening points → open.
Step 4: 10–12 HCP → Rule of 20. HCP + longest suit + second-longest suit ≥ 20 → open.
Step 5: neither → pass, unless the hand is a six-card weak two or a seven-card preempt (Lesson 6).

lessons.title: Opening 1♥ or 1♠
lessons.tip: A one-level major promises five or more cards. Equal length: higher ranking. 6–5: bid the six — even when the six is a minor (Lesson 3).
lessons.newHere: 1♥ and 1♠ promise five or more cards — and which suit to open when you are long in two.

revisits.what: opening points, the Rule of 20, and majors versus minors

teaching: The hand passed the strength test from Lesson 1 — 13+ opening points, or the Rule of 20 with at least 10 HCP. Now you pick a suit. In this system a 1♥ or 1♠ opening promises at least five cards in that major. Partner can raise with three-card support. That is the whole point of five-card majors.

Open your longest suit. With 5–5 or 6–6 in the majors, open the higher-ranking suit (spades), then bid hearts next — the suit rank order from Lesson 1 decides it. With 6–5, open the six, even if the five is the other major.
Strength first, always. Re-run Lesson 1's count before you look at the shape: a five-card major on a bust is a pass, not 1♥/1♠.

One thing to be clear about now, because it looks like an exception and is not. "Five-card major" is a promise about 1♥/1♠ — you may not open a major on four — not an instruction to prefer a major over a longer suit. The longest suit still wins. A major outranks both minors, so it takes every tie: five hearts and five diamonds opens 1♥. The only hand where a minor beats a five-card major is one where the minor is strictly longer — six diamonds beside five hearts opens 1♦. That is Lesson 3.
rules: 1♥ / 1♠ = 5+ cards and opening values (Lesson 1).
Open your longest suit. 5–5 or 6–6: higher ranking (1♠).
6–5: the six — and if the six is a minor, that is Lesson 3.

lessons.title: Opening 1♣ or 1♦
lessons.tip: Longest suit is a minor: open it — including a six-card minor beside a five-card major. No five-card suit at all: 1♦ on 4+, 1♣ on 3+. 4–4 minors: 1♦. 3–3 minors: 1♣.
lessons.newHere: When your longest suit is a minor — including when it beats a five-card major — and which minor to pick when nothing is five cards long.

revisits.what: opening points and the Rule of 20
open your longest suit, and the five-card promise 1♥/1♠ makes

teaching: Same rule as Lesson 2, other half of it: open your longest suit. Lesson 2 covered the hands where that suit is a major. Here it is a minor, and the bid is 1♦ or 1♣.

A long minor beats a five-card major. Six diamonds and five hearts opens 1♦, not 1♥. This surprises people, so be exact about why: 1♥/1♠ promises five cards — that is a floor on what the bid means, not a claim that a major jumps the queue. Length decides, and a major wins every tie because it outranks both minors. So the only hand where a minor wins is one where the minor is strictly longer. Five hearts and five diamonds: 1♥. Five hearts and six diamonds: 1♦. You bid the hearts next round, and partner hears both suits with the longer one named first.

Now the hands with no five-card suit anywhere. Some minor has to be opened, so the longer minor wins: 1♦ normally promises four diamonds, 1♣ is the catch-all and can be as short as three — it does not promise a real suit, it just starts the auction. Equal minors: 4–4 opens 1♦, 3–3 opens 1♣. With 4–4 in the majors you still open a minor, because Lesson 2 needs five; you show a major later. One shape to know: 4-4-3-2 with 4–4 majors and a doubleton club opens 1♦ on three, because some minor must be opened and diamonds is the longer one.

What waits until later, so it does not surprise you. A long minor beside a five-card major is awkward on the second round: after 1♦ – 1♠ from partner, naming the hearts costs the two-level and promises extra values, so it is only available on the stronger hands — though a 6–5 shape often gets there, because those length points from Lesson 1 count. Without them you rebid your diamonds and the hearts go unsaid for now. That bid has a name, the reverse, and it is Chapter 8. None of it changes the opening: you still open your longest suit.
rules: Open your longest suit (Lesson 2). When that suit is a minor, this lesson.
A minor beats a five-card major only when it is STRICTLY longer. 5♥/5♦ → 1♥. 5♥/6♦ → 1♦.
No five-card suit: longer minor wins. 1♦ = 4+, 1♣ = 3+. 4–4 minors: 1♦. 3–3 minors: 1♣.

lessons.title: Opening 1NT
lessons.tip: 15–17 balanced opens 1NT, including a five-card major. 14 with a five-card suit upgrades.
lessons.newHere: Balanced shape — 4333, 4432, 5332 — and the 1NT opening, which jumps ahead of the suit openings you learned in Lessons 2 and 3.

revisits.what: HCP, and length points — which 1NT does not use
opening a five-card major
opening a minor

teaching: A balanced hand is 4333, 4432, or 5332 — no singleton, no void, and not 5422 (two doubletons). This is the first shape test in the course that is not just “how long is my longest suit”, so learn the three patterns.

With 15–17 HCP and a balanced hand, open 1NT. This takes priority over Lessons 2 and 3: you open 1NT even when the five-card suit is a major, which is the one place the five-card-major rule is overruled. It keeps the strong hand hidden and avoids an awkward rebid.

Count HCP only for the 1NT range — no length points from Lesson 1, because 1NT is a high-card bid. One nudge upward: 14 HCP balanced with a five-card suit is treated as 1NT too. Below that, a balanced 12–14 goes back to Lessons 2 and 3 and opens a suit, and 5422 is not balanced at all, so it opens a suit as well.
rules: Balanced = 4333 / 4432 / 5332. 5422 is not balanced.
1NT = 15–17 HCP, balanced. HCP only — no length points (Lesson 1).
1NT beats a 5-card major (Lesson 2) — still 1NT.
14 HCP balanced with a 5-card suit upgrades to 1NT.
Balanced 12–14: open a suit (Lessons 2 and 3).

lessons.title: 2NT and strong 2♣
lessons.tip: 20–21 HCP balanced: 2NT — high cards only, and no five-card upgrade. Stronger than that: 2♣.
lessons.newHere: The two openings stronger than 1NT: 2NT for 20–21 balanced, and the artificial 2♣ for everything above — and which count each of them uses.

revisits.what: balanced shape, the 15–17 range this is too strong for, and the five-card upgrade that does NOT come up a range
length points, which 2♣ uses and 2NT does not

teaching: Same balanced shapes as Lesson 4, one range up: 20–21 HCP balanced opens 2NT. Partner reads the range straight off the bid, so there is nothing left to describe later.
22+ HCP, or 21+ opening points on an unbalanced hand, starts with 2♣. It is artificial and strong — it says nothing about clubs. Partner must respond, and the pair is in a game-forcing auction.

Count high cards for the 2NT range, and this time there is no nudge. Lesson 4 let a balanced 14 with a five-card suit come up to 1NT; that upgrade does not come up a range with it. Nineteen balanced is not a 2NT opening, five-card suit or no — you open the suit and jump to 2NT on the next round, which shows exactly 18–19, so nothing is lost by not upgrading. The five-card suit does not push a 21 out of the range either. 2NT is 20–21 high-card points, full stop.

So notice where the length points went, because they are not gone from this lesson — they are in the other bid. The second door into 2♣ is 21+ opening points on an unbalanced hand, and that count does include length: 20 HCP with 5-4-2-2 is 21 opening points and opens 2♣, while the same 20 HCP balanced opens 2NT. This is the split worth carrying forward. High-card points say which strength band you are in, because every bid above 1NT is defined in high cards. Length points say how many tricks you can make. A notrump opening asks the first question; 2♣ asks the second.
These hands are rare, and the test is nearly always the same one: is this balanced 20–21 (2NT), or is it stronger than that (2♣)?
rules: 2NT = 20–21 HCP, balanced (Lesson 4's shapes).
2NT counts HCP only — no length points, and no five-card upgrade. That upgrade is 1NT's alone.
2♣ = 22+ HCP, or 21+ opening points unbalanced — that door DOES count length. Artificial: not a club suit.
15–17 balanced is still 1NT (Lesson 4).

lessons.title: Weak twos and three-level preempts
lessons.tip: Six-card ♦/♥/♠ and 5–10 HCP: weak two. Seven-plus and 5–10: bid three. No weak 2♣, and no preempt in fourth seat.
lessons.newHere: Weak twos and three-level preempts: bidding on a hand Lesson 1 told you to pass, because the suit is long enough to be worth the space it steals — and the one seat where that trade stops paying.

revisits.what: the pass, and the exception this lesson finally drills
1♥/1♠ on a six-card major when you do have opening values

teaching: This is the exception flagged in Lesson 1. The hand is too weak to open at the one-level, but it has a long suit — so bid anyway and take away the opponents' room. A weak two shows exactly six diamonds, hearts or spades with 5–10 HCP.
There is no weak 2♣: 2♣ is already the strong artificial opening from Lesson 5, so a six-card club suit on a weak hand simply passes.
With seven or more cards in any suit — clubs included — and 5–10 HCP, and still not enough to open one: bid three of the suit. You are stealing space, not describing an opening hand.

Now the limit. A preempt is a trade: you risk playing a poor contract in exchange for bidding room the opponents no longer get. In fourth seat, with three passes already in front of you, there is no room left to buy — nobody is waiting to bid. So a preempt in fourth seat is all risk and no reward: pass, and let the deal be passed out. First, second and third seat still preempt as above.

Run Lesson 1's count first, every time. A six-card major with 13 opening points is 1♥/1♠ from Lesson 2, not a weak two — the preempt is only for hands that failed the opening test. A real opening hand still opens in fourth seat; it is only the preempt that goes away.
rules: Weak 2♦ / 2♥ / 2♠ = exactly six cards, 5–10 HCP, cannot open one (Lesson 1).
No weak 2♣ — 2♣ is the strong opening (Lesson 5).
7+ cards in any suit, 5–10 HCP, cannot open one: bid 3 of the suit.
Fourth seat (three passes in front): no preempt. Pass and let the deal be passed out.
Opening values first: a 6-card major with 13+ is 1♥/1♠ (Lesson 2), in any seat.

lessons.title: Pass, 2NT, or 3NT
lessons.tip: No four-card major: 0–7 pass, 8–9 invite 2NT, 10+ raise to 3NT. Count HCP only.
lessons.newHere: Your first lesson as responder: partner has already bid, you count HCP only, and with no long or four-card major you Pass, invite with 2NT, or bid 3NT.

revisits.what: what partner's 1NT promises: 15–17 balanced
HCP — which you now count without the length points

teaching: You are the responder now: partner opened 1NT, so from Lesson 4 you know they hold 15–17 HCP and a balanced hand. Add your HCP to theirs; about 25 between the two hands is enough for 3NT.
Count high-card points only. The length points from Lesson 1 were for deciding whether to open — opposite a notrump opening they do not apply.

This lesson deals only hands with no four-card major and no five-card major, because those shapes have better bids than notrump — the transfer in Lesson 8 and Stayman in Lesson 9. On the rest: 0–7 pass, 8–9 bid 2NT, 10+ bid 3NT. 2NT is an invitation, not a resting place — with 10 or more you must not park there.
rules: Partner's 1NT = 15–17 balanced (Lesson 4).
As responder to 1NT: HCP only, no length points.
No 4-card and no 5-card major: 0–7 Pass, 8–9 2NT, 10+ 3NT.
2NT is invitational. Do not park in 2NT with 10+.

lessons.title: Jacoby transfers
lessons.tip: Five or more in a major: 2♦ transfers to hearts, 2♥ transfers to spades. 5–5 majors: transfer to spades.
lessons.newHere: Jacoby transfers — your first artificial bid: 2♦ makes partner bid hearts, 2♥ makes partner bid spades, so the strong hand plays the contract.

revisits.what: the HCP-only count, and the Pass / 2NT / 3NT ladder this replaces
partner's 1NT: 15–17 HCP balanced

teaching: The shape Lesson 7 set aside: five or more cards in a major. Partner's 1NT promised a balanced hand (Lesson 4), so they hold at least two of your suit — that is a seven-card fit at worst and usually eight — and the cheaper major game from Lesson 1 is the contract you want.

So you do not bid your suit; you make partner bid it. With five or more hearts, bid 2♦ and partner must bid 2♥. With five or more spades, bid 2♥ and partner must bid 2♠. The bid is artificial — 2♦ says nothing about diamonds. Its whole purpose is to make the 1NT hand declarer, so their high cards sit behind the opening lead instead of in front of it.

The transfer says nothing about strength either. Weak, invitational and game-going hands all start with the same bid, and you describe how strong you are on the next round. That is why one bid covers so many hands.

5–5 in the majors: transfer to spades with 2♥ — the higher-ranking major, per Lesson 1's suit order — and you can still show hearts afterwards. 5–4 is not a transfer; that is Lesson 9's Stayman, because transferring would bury the four-card suit.
Partner has no choice about completing: 2♦ is always answered 2♥, and 2♥ always 2♠. Lesson 17 puts you in that chair.
rules: 5+ hearts → 2♦. 5+ spades → 2♥. Artificial — partner must complete.
5–5 majors → transfer to spades (2♥).
5–4 majors → Stayman instead (Lesson 9).
Partner completes: 2♦ → 2♥, 2♥ → 2♠, always (Lesson 17).

lessons.title: Stayman
lessons.tip: Eight or more HCP and a four-card major, with no five-card major to transfer: bid 2♣. 5–4 majors are Stayman too.
lessons.newHere: Stayman: 2♣ asks partner to name a four-card major — for the hands with a major too short to transfer.

revisits.what: the transfer, which takes priority whenever you hold five or more of a major
the Pass / 2NT / 3NT ladder for hands with no major at all
partner's 1NT: 15–17 HCP balanced

teaching: Two cases are settled. No major at all: Lesson 7's ladder — Pass, 2NT or 3NT. Five or more of a major: Lesson 8's transfer. This lesson is the gap between them — a four-card major, or five-four in the majors, which is not enough to claim the fit on your own.

With four cards you cannot know there is a fit: partner's balanced hand might hold two. So you ask. Stayman — 2♣ — is artificial like the transfer and shows no clubs; it asks whether partner holds a four-card major, so the pair can find the 4–4 or 5–3 fit and play the cheaper major game. Use it with 8+ HCP and at least one four-card major.

5–4 in the majors with 8+ is Stayman, not Lesson 8's transfer. Both suits are worth hearing about, and transferring would bury the four-card one — you want to find either fit, not just the longer suit.

Partner's answer, so you can read it when it comes: 2♥ with four hearts (even holding four spades too), 2♠ with four spades and no four hearts, 2♦ with neither. Hearts come first so the answer is never ambiguous. Lesson 17 puts you in the opener's chair for those.
Below 8 HCP, do not use Stayman as an escape from 1NT even with 4–4 majors — garbage Stayman is off in this tree. Those hands pass, as in Lesson 7.
rules: 8+ HCP and a 4-card major, no 5-card major → 2♣ Stayman. Artificial, not clubs.
5+ major → transfer instead (Lesson 8).
5–4 majors and 8+ → Stayman, not a transfer.
Partner answers 2♥ / 2♠ / 2♦, hearts first. You bid those in Lesson 17.
0–7 with 4–4 majors: pass (Lesson 7) — garbage Stayman is off.

lessons.title: Raising 1♥ or 1♠
lessons.tip: Three-card support: add shortage. 6–9 raise to 2, 10–12 jump to 3, 13+ bid game.
lessons.newHere: Fits and shortage points: three-card support makes a fit, and with a fit you count shortage — doubleton +1, singleton +3, void +5 — in place of length.

revisits.what: the five cards partner's 1♥/1♠ promised
HCP, and the length points that shortage now replaces

teaching: Partner opened 1♥ or 1♠, so from Lesson 2 they hold at least five. Three cards in that suit gives the pair eight — a fit — and a fit changes how you count. Add your HCP to shortage points: a doubleton +1, a singleton +3, a void +5. Short suits are worth something once you have trumps to ruff with, which is why length points from Lesson 1 step aside here.
With that total: 0–5 pass, even holding support — you are simply too weak. 6–9 raise to two. 10–12 jump to three, a limit raise. 13+ raise straight to game, 4♥ or 4♠.
Fit first. When you have a raise available, take it — the raise names the strain and the range in one call, and looking for something better only muddies it.
rules: 3+ cards in partner's major = a fit (they promised 5 — Lesson 2).
With a fit, count HCP + shortage: doubleton +1, singleton +3, void +5.
0–5 pass, 6–9 raise to 2, 10–12 jump to 3, 13+ raise to game.
A raise beats any other bid you might have.

lessons.title: A new suit over 1♥ or 1♠
lessons.tip: No fit? Show a suit of your own. One-level needs 6+ HCP; the two-level needs 10+.
lessons.newHere: Bidding a suit of your own when partner opened a major and you cannot raise — and why the two-level costs more than the one-level.

revisits.what: the raise, which comes first whenever you hold three-card support
suit rank — it decides which bids are cheap and which are not

teaching: Fewer than three cards in partner's major means Lesson 10's raise is off, and you need something else to say. The cheapest thing you can say is a suit at the one-level, and over 1♥ there is exactly one: 1♠. That shows four or more spades and 6+ HCP.

Over 1♠ there is nothing left at the one-level — spades is the top suit (Lesson 1), so any suit of yours costs a trip to the two-level. That is a real price: you are promising to make eight tricks instead of seven, and partner may have a minimum. So a new suit at the two-level needs 10+ HCP.

The two-level also wants a real suit. A new minor at the two-level needs four or more cards; a new major at the two-level needs five, because with only four you would have had the cheaper one-level bid available or a better route. 2♥ over 1♠ therefore promises five hearts and 10+.
A new suit is forcing for one round: partner must bid again. That is what makes it safe to introduce a suit rather than settle — you will get another turn.
rules: No 3-card support → no raise (Lesson 10).
New suit at the one-level (1♥–1♠) = 4+ cards, 6+ HCP.
New suit at the two-level = 10+ HCP.
Two-level new minor: 4+ cards. Two-level new major (2♥ over 1♠): 5+ cards.
A new suit is forcing for one round.

lessons.title: 1NT and pass over 1♥/1♠
lessons.tip: 6–9 with nothing else to say: 1NT. 0–5: pass and let partner play it.
lessons.newHere: The two answers left when you can neither raise nor bid a suit: the 1NT dustbin, and the pass that keeps you out of trouble.

revisits.what: the new-suit bids you try before falling back on notrump
the raise, which still comes first
the 1NT opening, which this 1NT response is not

teaching: Work down the list. No three-card support, so no raise (Lesson 10). Nothing worth bidding at the one-level and not enough for the two-level (Lesson 11). With 6–9 HCP you still owe partner a call, so respond 1NT.

Be clear about what this 1NT is not. It has nothing to do with the 15–17 opening from Lesson 4. As a response it is a dustbin: it means “I have a few points and no better call.” Partner will read it that way and bid on accordingly.

With 0–5 HCP and no fit, pass. This is the hardest habit to learn, because passing feels like giving up — but partner opened on as few as 13 points, and keeping the auction alive on a bust just pushes you into a contract neither of you can make. Partner may well have a playable spot at the one-level already.
So the full order over partner's major: raise if you have a fit; bid a suit if you have one you can afford; 1NT with 6–9 and nothing else; pass with 0–5.
rules: Order: raise (Lesson 10) → new suit (Lesson 11) → 1NT → pass.
6–9, no fit, nothing biddable: 1NT — a dustbin, not Lesson 4’s opening.
0–5, no fit: Pass.

lessons.title: Show a major over 1♣/1♦
lessons.tip: Partner’s minor may be short. With 6+ HCP and a four-card major, bid it. 4–4 majors: the cheaper (1♥).
lessons.newHere: Responding to an opening that may not be a real suit: with a minor opening, finding a major fit is your job, not partner’s.

revisits.what: 1♣ on as few as three cards, 1♦ on four
the one-level new suit at 6+ HCP

teaching: Everything changes when partner opens a minor. From Lesson 3, 1♣ can be three cards and 1♦ can be four — neither is a described suit, and neither is where you want to play. Compare Lesson 10, where 1♥/1♠ promised five and your first thought was whether you had a fit. Here your first thought is a major of your own.

With 6+ HCP and a four-card major, bid it at the one-level. Four is enough — you are not claiming a fit, you are asking whether partner has one, and partner can raise with four. This is how the pair reaches the cheap major game from Lesson 1 even though nobody opened a major.

4–4 in the majors: bid the cheaper one, 1♥. That keeps 1♠ available on the next round, so the pair can check both majors for the price of one. Longer major first when they are unequal; 5–5 or 6–6, bid the higher (1♠) as in Lesson 2.
A major beats a minor raise and it beats notrump, even when the minor fit is real. The major is worth more tricks and the auction is still cheap — there is time to come back to the minor.
rules: Partner’s minor may be short (Lesson 3) — a major of your own comes first.
4+ major and 6+ HCP: bid it at the one-level.
4–4 majors: cheaper (1♥). Unequal: longer. 5–5: higher (1♠).
A major outranks a minor raise and outranks notrump.

lessons.title: No major over 1♣/1♦
lessons.tip: 1♦ over 1♣ with diamonds. Six clubs and 10+ over 1♦: 2♣. Otherwise 1NT or pass.
lessons.newHere: What to bid over a minor when you have no four-card major: the 1♦ reply, the 2♣ shift on a long club suit, and the 1NT/pass floor.

revisits.what: the major you bid first when you have one
the two-level new suit and its 10+ HCP price
the 1NT dustbin and the pass on a bust

teaching: No four-card major, so Lesson 13's answer is unavailable. Over 1♣ the cheapest useful call is 1♦, which shows four or more diamonds and 6+ HCP, and denies a four-card major — partner learns two things for one bid.

Over 1♦ that reply does not exist, because diamonds is partner's suit. The suit you might have instead is clubs, and clubs is a level higher: 2♣. That is a two-level new suit, so it costs 10+ HCP exactly as in Lesson 11, and it wants a real suit rather than four small ones — which here means six. Work it out: you have no four-card major and no diamond fit, so the majors hold three at most and so do the diamonds. Four or five clubs would leave you 4-3-3-3 or 5-3-3-2, and both of those are flat hands that belong in notrump. Only six clubs makes the shape worth the extra level.

Raising the minor needs real length — five clubs to raise 1♣, four diamonds to raise 1♦ — and even then it is a part-score bid, because eleven tricks is a long way. Do not chase five of a minor when notrump will do.

The floor is the same as Lesson 12: 6–9 with no major, no raise and nothing at the two-level responds 1NT, and 0–5 passes. With 10–12 balanced, invite with 2NT. With 13+ HCP and a minor fit, bid 3NT: nine tricks in notrump are far cheaper than eleven in a minor, and that stays true even when your shape is a little awkward. Only an unbalanced 16+ is worth the eleven-trick game at 5♣ or 5♦. A jump to three of the minor therefore means 10–12 — or 13 points that came from a short suit rather than from honours — and never more, so partner can read it.
rules: No 4-card major (Lesson 13) → work down this list.
1♣–1♦ = 4+ diamonds, 6+ HCP, and no 4-card major.
1♦–2♣ = 6+ clubs and 10+ HCP (two-level price, Lesson 11).
Raise a minor only with real length: 5+ clubs over 1♣, 4+ diamonds over 1♦.
6–9 nothing else: 1NT. 0–5: Pass. 10–12 balanced: 2NT. 13+ HCP with a fit: 3NT, or 5m when unbalanced with 16+. A jump to 3m means 10–12.

lessons.title: After partner raises your major
lessons.tip: Minimum pass. Extra values invite. A big hand bids game. Same idea over a limit raise: pass or go.
lessons.newHere: Your first lesson as opener bidding a second time: partner has limited their hand, so you decide how high — pass, invite, or bid game.

revisits.what: the raise ranges partner is showing you
opening points — HCP + length, which you count again here

teaching: Partner raised your major, so the fit is confirmed and the strain is settled. All that remains is the level, and you own that decision because partner's raise named a narrow range. Count your opening points again — HCP plus length, from Lesson 1.
A simple raise (1♠–2♠) was 6–9 in Lesson 10. With 13–15 pass and play there. With 16–18 raise one more as an invitation. With 19–20 bid the game yourself.
A limit raise (1♠–3♠) was 10–12, and is already an invitation — partner has handed you the decision. With a minimum, pass. With extras, bid game.
Do not introduce a new suit here. The fit is found; the only open question is how high.
rules: Count opening points: HCP + length (Lesson 1).
After a simple raise (partner 6–9, Lesson 10): 13–15 pass, 16–18 raise one, 19–20 bid game.
After a limit raise (partner 10–12): minimum pass, extras bid game.
No new suits — the strain is settled.

lessons.title: After partner’s 1NT
lessons.tip: 1NT is not forcing. Pass a 5332 minimum, rebid six cards, or show a four-card side suit.
lessons.newHere: Rebidding over partner's 1NT response: it is not forcing, so pass a flat minimum, rebid a six-card suit, or show a four-card side suit.

revisits.what: the 1NT response — 6–9 HCP with no fit for your major
balanced shape, which decides whether you pass here

teaching: Partner's 1NT was the dustbin from Lesson 12: 6–9 HCP, no three-card support for your major. It is not forcing, so passing is a real option and often the right one — with a 5332 minimum, pass and play 1NT.
With a six-card major, rebid it (2♥ or 2♠). Partner holds at most two, but six against two still usually plays better than notrump, and partner can now choose.
With a four-card side suit, bid that suit at the two-level. That is a shape bid inside the minimum range, not a claim of extra strength.
Do not rebid a five-card suit. Partner already heard it and declined to support it, and a 5332 minimum belongs in notrump.
rules: Partner's 1NT = 6–9, no fit (Lesson 12). Not forcing.
5332 minimum: pass.
Six-card suit: rebid it.
Four-card side suit: bid it at the two-level.
Never rebid a five-card suit.

lessons.title: Completing Stayman and transfers
lessons.tip: Stayman: show four hearts first, else four spades, else 2♦. Transfers: always complete.
lessons.newHere: The opener's side of transfers and Stayman — the answers to the asks you made in Lessons 8 and 9.

revisits.what: the 2♦ / 2♥ transfers you are now completing
the 2♣ Stayman ask you are now answering
your own 1NT opening, 15–17 balanced

teaching: You opened 1NT. If partner transferred (Lesson 8), complete it: 2♥ over 2♦, 2♠ over 2♥. Always, with no exceptions — there is no super-accept in this tree, so extra strength and four-card support change nothing.

If partner bid 2♣ — Stayman, from Lesson 9 — answer in strict priority: 2♥ with four hearts, even when you also hold four spades; 2♠ with four spades and no four hearts; 2♦ with neither. The hearts-first order is what lets partner read your answer without ambiguity.

These calls are mechanical, which is the point: partner is asking, and the answer never depends on how much you like your hand. The test is the priority order, and remembering that a transfer is not optional.
rules: Transfer (Lesson 8): 2♦ → always 2♥. 2♥ → always 2♠.
Stayman (Lesson 9): 2♥ with 4 hearts (even with 4 spades); 2♠ with 4 spades and no 4 hearts; else 2♦.
No super-accept. Extras do not change the answer.

lessons.title: After a new suit
lessons.tip: Raise partner’s major with four-card support. Otherwise 1NT on a balanced minimum.
lessons.newHere: Rebidding after partner's new suit: raise their major with four-card support, otherwise 1NT on a balanced minimum.

revisits.what: partner's one-level major response over your minor
your own 1♣ / 1♦ opening
the 15–17 1NT opening, which this rebid is not

teaching: You opened a minor (Lesson 3) and partner answered with a major at the one-level (Lesson 13), which promised four cards and 6+ HCP. With four-card support and a minimum, raise to two — that names the eight-card fit at a level that is safe on minimum values.

Without support, a balanced minimum rebids 1NT. Note that this shows 12–14 balanced, not the 15–17 of Lesson 4's 1NT opening — the strong hands opened 1NT in the first place, so a 1NT rebid can only be the weaker one.
Chapter 8 takes this further: partner's new suit is forcing, and there is a priority list for finding the right rebid on any hand. This lesson is the simplest case of it.
rules: Partner's one-level major = 4+ cards, 6+ HCP (Lesson 13).
Four-card support and a minimum: raise to two.
Balanced minimum, no fit: rebid 1NT — 12–14, not Lesson 4's 15–17.

lessons.title: After partner's one-level suit
lessons.tip: A new suit is forcing — you must bid. Four-card major first, then support, then 1NT.
lessons.newHere: The first rule that takes a choice away from you: a new suit by partner is forcing for one round, so opener must bid again — and the order in which to look for something to say.

revisits.what: the new suit partner bid, and that it is forcing
the 1♦ response over 1♣
opening points — the strength bands below are counted the same way

teaching: Lessons 11 and 14 said a new suit is forcing for one round, and this is the lesson where that matters to you. Partner has bid a suit at the one level. You may not pass — partner is entitled to another turn, and passing would strand a hand that could be worth game.

Work down a fixed list. First: can you show a four-card major at the one level? After 1♣ – 1♦ you can bid 1♥ or 1♠, and you should, because it is still the cheapest level and it is the only chance at the major game from Lesson 1. Hearts before spades when you hold both four-card majors.

Second: do you have four-card support for partner's suit? Raise it. With a minimum raise to two; with 16–18 opening points jump a level to invite; and after 1♥ – 1♠, with 19–20, bid 4♠ outright. The raise names the fit and the range in one call, exactly as partner's raise did in Lesson 10.
Third: do you have six cards in the suit you opened? Repeat it. Partner may hold a doubleton, and six against two usually plays better than notrump.

Last: notrump, by strength. A balanced minimum rebids 1NT — 12–14, since a stronger balanced hand would have opened 1NT (Lesson 4). A balanced 18–19 jumps to 2NT instead, which is how you show extras without a fit and without a long suit.
rules: A new suit by partner is forcing for one round — never pass it.
1. Four-card major at the one level: bid it (hearts before spades).
2. Four-card support: raise. Minimum → 2, 16–18 → 3, 19–20 → 4 of a major.
3. Six cards in your own suit: rebid it.
4. Balanced minimum: 1NT (12–14). Balanced 18–19: 2NT.

lessons.title: After partner's two-level suit
lessons.tip: Partner promised 10+, so game is close. Fit first, then your own six, then 2NT on a minimum or 3NT with extras.
lessons.newHere: Rebidding when partner has promised 10+ HCP: the same priority list as the one-level case, but every fallback moves up a level because the pair is already close to game.

revisits.what: the priority list — support, then your own suit, then notrump
the two-level new suit and its 10+ HCP promise
the 2♣ response over 1♦

teaching: Partner bid a new suit at the two level, which from Lesson 11 promised 10+ HCP and a real suit. Add that to your own opening 13 and the pair has around 23 — a trick or two short of game, but close enough that you must not sign off cheaply. Same priority list as Lesson 19; every rung sits a level higher.

Support first. Partner's two-level major promised five cards, so three of them is a fit: raise to three on a minimum, and bid the game with 16+ opening points. Partner's two-level minor promised four, so you need four: raise to three on a minimum, and with 16+ bid 3NT rather than chase eleven tricks in the minor.

No fit? Six cards in your own suit means you repeat it. In every one of these auctions your suit ranks above partner's — that is what made their bid a two-level bid in the first place — so repeating it costs nothing and stays a minimum action.

Otherwise notrump, and here the strength band does the talking. A minimum bids 2NT: it keeps the auction alive without promising anything, and partner with 10+ decides where to play. With 16+ opening points bid 3NT — partner's 10 plus your 16 is game, and with no fit either way notrump is where nine tricks are cheapest.
rules: A two-level new suit promises 10+ HCP. Never pass it.
3-card support for partner’s major: raise to 3, or bid game with 16+.
4-card support for partner’s minor: raise to 3, or bid 3NT with 16+.
Six cards in your own suit: rebid it at the two level (it always outranks partner’s).
No fit: 2NT on a minimum, 3NT with 16+.

lessons.title: Accepting and declining invitations
lessons.tip: An invitation you may pass — but decide on your hand, not by reflex. Top of your range: accept.
lessons.newHere: The other half of opener’s job: when partner has limited their hand rather than forced you, passing becomes legal — and the choice between passing and accepting is a strength count, not a habit.

revisits.what: the forcing bids you were not allowed to pass
the 2NT invitation partner is making here
the minor raise and the 1NT response

teaching: Lessons 19 and 20 were about bids you may not pass. This lesson is the mirror: partner has limited their hand instead of forcing you, so passing is a legal choice — and that makes it a decision, which is the part people get wrong. A pass here must come from counting your hand, not from partner having stopped bidding.

Partner's 2NT is the invitation from Lesson 7: 8–9 HCP asking whether you have enough for game. After your 1NT opening you hold 15–17, so the arithmetic is simple — 15 is a minimum, so pass; 16 or 17 is the top of your range, so accept and bid 3NT. Over a suit opening the same question arrives from a 10–12 hand, and there you accept with 14 or more.

Partner's raise of your minor is limited too: a simple raise is 6–9 and a limit raise is 10–12. With a minimum, pass and play the part-score — five of a minor is eleven tricks and rarely worth it. With 16–18 opposite a simple raise, try 2NT. With enough for game, bid 3NT rather than 5♣ or 5♦.

Partner's 1NT response to your minor is 6–9 with no four-card major (Lesson 14), and it is not forcing. Pass it on a balanced minimum. With six or more in the suit you opened, rebid the suit — partner has denied a major and may be short in yours. With 18–19 balanced, jump to 2NT.
The habit to build: every time partner's bid could be passed, count first. The question is never “has partner stopped?” — it is “am I at the top or the bottom of what I promised?”
rules: An invitation may be passed — but only after counting your hand.
Partner’s 2NT over your 1NT: pass with 15, bid 3NT with 16–17.
Partner’s 2NT over your suit opening: accept with 14+.
Minor raise: minimum passes. 16–18 over a simple raise tries 2NT. Game values bid 3NT, not 5m.
Partner’s 1NT over your minor: pass a balanced minimum, rebid a 6-card suit, jump to 2NT with 18–19.

lessons.title: Responding to 2♣ and 2NT
lessons.tip: 2♣ can never be passed — 2♦ waits. Over 2NT: Stayman and transfers a level up, 3NT with 5+.
lessons.newHere: The first bid in the course you are forbidden to pass, and the waiting bid that answers it — plus 2NT, where the familiar 1NT machinery moves up a level and the thresholds drop.

revisits.what: the 2♣ and 2NT openings you are now on the other side of
the transfers, which work the same way one level higher
the Stayman ask, likewise

teaching: Lesson 5 taught you to open 2♣ on 22+ HCP or 21+ opening points unbalanced. This is the other side of it, and it comes with a rule the course has not needed until now: 2♣ is game-forcing, so you may not pass it. Not on 5 HCP, not on nothing. Partner has a hand that can make game opposite a blank, and passing throws it away.

So there must be a bid that means “I have nothing”, and that is 2♦. It says nothing whatever about diamonds — it is a waiting bid, keeping the auction as low as possible so partner has room to describe the monster. Bid it on 0–7 HCP whatever your shape.

With 8 or more you make a positive response: name a five-card suit if you have one (2♥, 2♠, 3♣ or 3♦), or bid 2NT with no five-card suit. A positive tells partner the pair is looking at a slam, not just a game, so it is worth showing straight away.

2NT is a different animal — it is natural and limited, 20–21 balanced, so you are allowed to pass it. Everything you learned over 1NT applies one level up: 3♣ is Stayman, 3♦ transfers to hearts and 3♥ to spades, exactly as in Lessons 8 and 9 — including the exception, that 5–4 in the majors is Stayman rather than a transfer, so the four-card suit is not buried.

What changes over 2NT is the arithmetic. Partner holds 20–21 rather than 15–17, so game needs far less from you: 5 HCP with no four-card major is already 3NT. Stayman needs that same 5, because over 2NT there is no invitational step — the next rung up is the game itself — so a hand that asks must be able to answer. With less than 5 you may still transfer, since a transfer only names a suit and never asks a question. Only 0–4 with no long major passes.
rules: 2♣ is game-forcing. Never pass it.
0–7 over 2♣: bid 2♦ — waiting, and nothing to do with diamonds.
8+ with a 5-card suit: name it. 8+ without one: 2NT.
Over 2NT: 3♣ Stayman, 3♦ → hearts, 3♥ → spades (Lessons 8 and 9).
Over 2NT: 5–4 majors is 3♣ Stayman, not a transfer (as over 1NT).
Over 2NT: 5+ HCP is 3NT. 0–4 with no long major passes.

lessons.title: Responding to a weak two or a preempt
lessons.tip: Partner told you the hand exactly. Over a weak two: raise to obstruct, or bid game with 16+. Over a preempt: game or pass.
lessons.newHere: Captaincy: partner has described the hand almost exactly, so the whole decision is yours — and a raise here obstructs rather than invites.

revisits.what: the weak two and the three-level preempt you are answering
raising a major, which meant something quite different

teaching: A weak two says six cards and 5–10 HCP. A three-level preempt says seven or more and 5–10. Either way partner has spent one bid describing the hand almost exactly, which puts the whole decision on you — that is what being the captain means, and it is the opposite of Lesson 10, where partner's 1♥ or 1♠ left the strength open.

Add your hand to what partner promised. With 16 or more and three-card support for the major, that is roughly 25 combined: bid the game. With 16+ and no fit, you still have game values — over a weak two, bid a five-card suit of your own if you have one, which is forcing and leaves room to find the right game; otherwise bid 3NT, because partner's long suit supplies the tricks once your stoppers hold.

Below that, with support, raise anyway — but only over a weak two, and understand what the raise is doing. It is not an invitation, and partner must not take it as one. Raising 2♠ to 3♠ takes another level away from the opponents while your extra trump makes the higher contract safe. Over a three-level preempt there is no such bid: the next level up is already game, so there is nothing to obstruct with. You either have game values or you pass.

With no fit and no game, pass. This is the hardest one, because a 12-count feels like too much to give up on. It is not: partner's 5–10 plus your 12 is nowhere near game, and moving only tells the opponents where the cards are.

From the opener's chair the rule is even simpler. You already described the hand, so you do not bid again — whatever partner chooses is the contract. The one exception is a new suit from partner, which is forcing; then you raise their major with three-card support, or repeat your own suit.
rules: Weak two = 6 cards, 5–10. Preempt = 7+, 5–10. You are the captain (Lesson 6).
16+ with 3-card support for the major: bid game.
16+ with no fit: over a weak two, a 5-card suit of your own (forcing); otherwise 3NT.
Over a weak two only, support without game values raises to obstruct — it is not an invitation.
Over a 3-level preempt there is no obstructive raise: the next level up is already game.
No fit, no game: pass and believe partner.
As opener: do not bid again — unless partner bids a new suit, which is forcing.

lessons.title: Rebidding after 2♣, 2NT or a preempt
lessons.tip: After 2♣ describe the monster. After 2NT answer the ask. After a preempt, say nothing.
lessons.newHere: The opener’s side of Chapter 9 — and the clearest case in the course of when to keep describing a hand and when to stop.

revisits.what: the waiting bid and the positives you are answering
the captaincy rule, from the other chair
completing Stayman and transfers over 1NT

teaching: Three openings, three completely different jobs, and the contrast is the lesson. After 2♣ you have told partner only that the hand is huge, so every rebid describes it further. After 2NT you have already described it, so you simply answer what partner asked. After a preempt you described it with the opening bid itself, so you say nothing more.

Over partner's 2♦ waiting bid, show your shape. Balanced 22–24 bids 2NT and balanced 25+ bids 3NT — those two calls pin the hand almost exactly. Unbalanced, name your longest suit at the cheapest level; the auction is forcing to game, so there is all the room you need.

Over 2NT, Stayman and the transfers are answered exactly as in Lesson 17, one level up. 3♥ with four hearts even holding four spades, 3♠ with four spades and no four hearts, 3♦ with neither; and a transfer is completed always, without exception.

Over a weak two or a preempt, pass whatever partner chose. Partner knows both hands better than you do, because your opening told them the shape and the range and their own hand told them the rest. Bidding again describes nothing and only raises the level. The single exception is a new suit, which is forcing: raise their major with three-card support, otherwise repeat your own suit.
rules: After 2♣ – 2♦: 2NT with 22–24 balanced, 3NT with 25+, else name your longest suit.
After 2♣ and a positive: raise partner’s major to game with 3-card support.
After 2NT: answer Stayman hearts-first, and always complete a transfer (Lesson 17).
After a weak two or preempt: pass whatever partner chose.
The exception: partner’s new suit is forcing — raise their major, or repeat your suit.
